title: Continuous integration with GitHub Actions
goal: Run lint, tests and builds automatically on every push and pull request.

concepts: CI: every change is checked automatically before it's merged
GitHub Actions: workflows, jobs, steps, runners, triggers (push, pull_request)
actions/checkout and actions/setup-node with npm caching
A matrix or separate jobs for api and web
Running the Firestore emulator (and a Postgres service container) in CI
Branch protection: require checks to pass before merging; status badges

resources.title: GitHub Actions: Building and testing Node.js

build.task: In standupboard: add .github/workflows/ci.yml that runs on push and pull_request: job api (npm ci, lint, typecheck, tests), job web (npm ci, lint, tests, production build), and job rules (install the Firebase CLI and run the rules tests with firebase emulators:exec). Cache npm dependencies. Protect main so all three jobs must pass before merging, and add the CI badge to the README. Do the same for applytrack, with a postgres service container for its DB tests. Open a pull request that deliberately breaks a test, watch CI fail, fix it, then merge.

starterFiles.name: .github/workflows/ci.yml
starterFiles.content:
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  api:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: api
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: api/package-lock.json
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test

  # TODO: web job (lint, test, build)
  # TODO: rules job (firebase emulators:exec)

acceptance: CI runs on every push and pull request with api, web and rules jobs
npm cache configured; runs finish in a few minutes
main is protected; failing checks block merging
A deliberately failing pull request was opened, fixed and merged
CI badges in both READMEs; ApplyTrack CI includes the Postgres DB tests

hints: Rules job: run npm i -g firebase-tools, then firebase emulators:exec --only firestore --project demo-test 'npm run test:rules'. A project id starting with demo- needs no real Firebase project or credentials.

Postgres in CI: services: postgres: { image: postgres:16, env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres }, ports: ['5432:5432'], options: --health-cmd pg_isready --health-interval 5s }, then set DATABASE_URL in the job's env.
The Firestore emulator needs Java; ubuntu-latest runners already include it.
proof: Link to a green CI run and to the pull request that failed first.

explainBack.q: What problem does CI solve for a team?
Why use a demo- project id for the rules tests in CI?

lastHintExplanation: CI runs the same checks on a clean machine for every change, so 'it works on my machine' problems and broken tests are caught before they reach main, and branch protection makes that mandatory. A demo- project id tells the Firebase emulator not to contact any real project, so CI needs no secrets and can never touch production data.

title: Deploying StandupBoard (and a Forgejo mirror bonus)
goal: Ship StandupBoard to production with a deploy pipeline, and optionally mirror your code to a self-hosted Git server.

concepts: Firebase Hosting for the Angular app (free tier); rewrites for SPA routing
The Express API on Coolify (or any free container host) with the service account as a secret
Separate Firebase projects or emulators for dev and production
Deploying from GitHub Actions after CI passes (needs: [ci jobs])
Bonus: Forgejo, a free self-hosted Git forge; push mirrors to keep a copy of your repos

build.task: Deploy StandupBoard: the web app on Firebase Hosting (firebase init hosting with the SPA rewrite to /index.html), Firestore rules deployed from the repo, the Express API on Coolify (or another host) with FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT and CORS settings as platform secrets. Add a deploy workflow that runs only on main after CI passes and deploys hosting and rules with a service account stored in GitHub secrets. Add your production domain to Firebase authorised domains. Seed a demo team and two demo accounts listed in the README. Bonus: run Forgejo on your Coolify server (or use a free Codeberg account, which runs Forgejo) and set up a push mirror of standupboard and applytrack. Write docs/deployment.md.
acceptance: Web app live on Firebase Hosting; deep links work
API live with HTTPS; secrets only in the platform and GitHub secrets
Deploys happen automatically from main only after CI passes
Production domain authorised for sign-in; Google sign-in works live
Demo accounts in the README; docs/deployment.md complete
Bonus: a working Forgejo or Codeberg mirror

hints: In the deploy workflow, use needs: [api, web, rules] in the same workflow, or trigger on workflow_run of CI with conclusion == 'success'.

A push mirror is configured on the source side: in GitHub, add a workflow that pushes to the mirror, or in Forgejo create a pull mirror that fetches from GitHub on a schedule. A pull mirror is simplest.
proof: Live URLs for the web app and API (and the mirror link if you did the bonus).

explainBack.q: Why should deploys only run after CI passes?
Why might a developer keep a mirror of their repos on a self-hosted forge?

lastHintExplanation: Making deploys depend on CI means a red test stops a broken build reaching users, with no human needing to remember. A mirror on Forgejo or Codeberg keeps a full copy of your history outside GitHub, which protects against account problems and shows you can run your own infrastructure.

hints: Structure: 'I'm a full-stack developer working with Angular, Node and PostgreSQL. Over the last six months I built … My strongest project is … I'm looking for a role where …'

explainBack.q: Deliver your 'tell me about yourself' answer now.

lastHintExplanation: Most first rounds start with 'tell me about yourself' and a project discussion. A rehearsed, structured answer (present, past, future) shows clarity and confidence. STAR stories with specific results are easy to follow and believable. Asking good questions shows you're evaluating the company too.

title: JavaScript and TypeScript interview questions
goal: Answer the most common JavaScript and TypeScript interview questions clearly, with small code examples.

concepts: Scope, hoisting, the temporal dead zone (var vs let vs const)
Closures and a practical use (private state, once(), memoize)
this: in methods, arrow functions, and call/apply/bind
The event loop: call stack, microtasks (promises) vs macrotasks (setTimeout)
== vs ===, truthy/falsy, reference vs value copying (shallow vs deep)
Prototypes and classes; TypeScript: interface vs type, generics, unknown vs any, utility types

build.task: In jobready-journey, create interview/js-questions.md with 25 questions and answers in your own words, each with a tiny code example you have run. Include output-prediction questions (event loop order, closures in loops with var vs let, this in callbacks). Then implement from scratch, with tests: debounce, throttle, once, memoize, deepClone (objects, arrays, Dates), a simple Promise.all, and a curry function. Time yourself: 15 minutes each.

starterFiles.name: interview/predict.js

acceptance: 25 questions answered in your own words with run examples
predict.js output predicted correctly (or the mistake explained)
7 utility functions implemented with tests
Each utility built in about 15 minutes
You can explain the event loop with a diagram

hints: predict.js prints 1, 5, 7, 3, 4, 6, 2, then 'var 3' three times, then 'let 0', 'let 1', 'let 2'. Work out why before you check.
Promise.all: return a new Promise; track results by index and a count of resolved values; reject on the first rejection; resolve when count === length (and immediately for an empty array).
Interviewers care about the explanation as much as the code. Practise saying 'the callback closes over the variable, not its value' and similar sentences aloud.
proof: Commit with js-questions.md and the utilities with tests.

explainBack.q: Explain why predict.js prints in that order.
lookFor: await schedules the rest as a microtask

explainBack.q: Why does the var loop print 3 three times but the let loop prints 0, 1, 2?
lookFor: var is function-scoped, one shared variable
let creates a new binding per iteration

lastHintExplanation: Synchronous code runs first (1, then 5 inside the async function up to await, then 7). Next, the microtask queue drains in order: 3, 4, then 6, which was scheduled by await. Only then does the setTimeout macrotask print 2. With var there's one shared i, which is 3 by the time the timers run; let creates a fresh j for each iteration.

predict.q: const a = { x: 1 }; const b = { ...a }; b.x = 2; console.log(a.x)
predict.why: Spread makes a shallow copy; changing b.x doesn't affect a.
== coerces [] to '' and then to 0, which equals false; === compares types.

title: Angular, backend and SQL interview questions
goal: Prepare clear answers to the framework, API and database questions junior full-stack interviews ask most.

concepts: Angular: components, signals vs RxJS, change detection, DI and providers, lifecycle hooks, routing and guards, forms, interceptors, lazy loading, @defer
HTML/CSS: semantic HTML, the box model, flexbox vs grid, specificity, responsive design, accessibility basics
Backend: REST, status codes, middleware, authentication vs authorisation, JWT vs sessions, CORS, validation
SQL: joins, GROUP BY/HAVING, indexes, transactions and ACID, normalisation, SQL injection
Firebase: when to use it, security rules, real-time listeners

build.task: In jobready-journey, write interview/stack-questions.md with 40 questions and answers in your own words, about 10 each for Angular, HTML/CSS, backend/API and SQL, each linked to a place in your own projects where you used the idea (e.g. 'Interceptors: ApplyTrack web/src/app/core/auth.interceptor.ts'). Then write 10 SQL queries from scratch against the ApplyTrack schema (e.g. the second most recent application per user, companies with more than 2 rejections, the average days from Applied to Interview) and check them in psql.
acceptance: 40 questions across 4 areas, in your own words
Each answer points to real code in your projects
10 SQL queries run successfully against ApplyTrack data
Includes at least one window-function query (ROW_NUMBER or LAG)
You can answer 'signals vs RxJS' and 'JWT vs sessions' without notes

hints: Linking answers to your code is powerful in interviews: 'I used a functional interceptor in ApplyTrack to attach the token and handle 401s globally.'
Second most recent per user: SELECT * FROM (SELECT a.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY applied_on DESC) AS rn FROM applications a) t WHERE rn = 2;
Days from Applied to Interview: join application_status_history to itself on application_id, where one row's to_status is Applied and the other's is Interview, then AVG the date difference.
proof: Commit with stack-questions.md and the SQL file.

explainBack.q: Signals vs RxJS in Angular: when do you use each?
lookFor: signals for synchronous state and derived values
RxJS for event streams, async, cancellation (debounce, switchMap)

explainBack.q: Explain a database transaction and ACID with an example from your projects.

lastHintExplanation: Signals hold state: current values, with computed values derived automatically. RxJS models streams of events over time, with operators for timing, cancellation and combining, which is why search uses debounceTime and switchMap. A transaction groups changes so they all happen or none do (atomicity). ApplyTrack's status update plus history insert is a perfect example to give.

title: Mock interview 1: technical round
goal: Experience a realistic technical interview, then turn the feedback into a focused plan.

concepts: Typical junior full-stack round: intro (5 min), project discussion (15), concepts (15), live coding (20), your questions (5)
Thinking aloud during coding: clarify, give examples, state the approach, code, test
Handling nerves: slow down, restate the question, it's fine to pause
Free mock interview options: peers, mentors, communities, Pramp-style platforms

resources.title: Tech Interview Handbook: Coding interview cheatsheet

build.task: Do a 60-minute mock interview with a real person if at all possible (friend in tech, mentor, college senior, or a peer-to-peer mock platform). Give them interview/mock1-script.md beforehand: your intro, questions about ApplyTrack, 6 concept questions (from Days 148–149), and one live coding task (e.g. 'group anagrams' or 'build a debounced search box'). If no one is available, record yourself answering on video with a timer. Afterwards write interview/mock1-review.md: scores 1–5 for communication, problem solving, code quality and project knowledge; the 3 weakest answers rewritten; and a 6-day plan for the final week.
acceptance: A 60-minute mock done with a person, or recorded
Script shared with the interviewer beforehand
Live coding done while thinking aloud
mock1-review.md with honest scores and 3 rewritten answers
A concrete plan for the final week

hints: Live coding framework: 1) restate the problem, 2) ask about edge cases, 3) walk through an example, 4) explain the approach and its complexity, 5) code, 6) test with the example and edge cases.
Ask your mock interviewer to interrupt with follow-ups ('what if the input is huge?'), as real interviewers do.
Recording yourself is uncomfortable but very effective. You'll notice filler words and unclear explanations at once.

explainBack.q: What was your weakest moment in the mock, and what's your improved answer?
Describe your live coding process step by step.

lastHintExplanation: Interviewers judge how you think as much as whether you finish. A repeatable process (restate, clarify edge cases, walk through an example, explain the approach, code, then test) keeps you calm and shows structured thinking even when you get stuck. Honest scoring and rewritten answers turn one mock into real improvement.
